## Paper

## Abstract

The contribution of airway pathobionts to chronic respiratory disease is increasingly recognized, yet the evolutionary processes that shift commensals to pathogens remain poorly understood. Here we investigate how antibiotic pressure drives adaptation in Neisseria subflava, a common airway commensal associated with bronchiectasis. Using serial passage under ceftriaxone exposure, we observe a >300-fold increase in resistance, accompanied by enhanced biofilm formation and genetic reprogramming. Whole-genome sequencing reveals recurrent mutations in the adhesin gene ataA, while single-cell transcriptomics identifies six functionally distinct clusters indicating adaptive programs in growth, metal homeostasis, oxidative stress, and cell-wall remodeling. Notably, biofilm integrity is maintained through compensatory upregulation of comP and bamE, which promotes phagocytic evasion and resistance in experimentally evolved strains and clinical isolates. Iron availability further stabilizes biofilm and modulates antibiotic tolerance, underscoring metal homeostasis as a contributory adaptive axis. Together, these findings reveal a multifaceted strategy by which N. subflava exploits antibiotic selection to transition towards pathogenicity. By integrating experimental evolution with single-cell resolution, we establish a framework for understanding the commensal-to-pathobiont transition, with broad implications for the airway microbiome and antimicrobial resistance in chronic respiratory disease.

---

## Introduction

The dynamic interplay between host and microbiome has reshaped our understanding of airway pathology, highlighting the microbiome as a critical determinant of respiratory health and disease1–3. Advances in high-throughput molecular profiling and computation have enabled holistic analyses of airway microbial communities2,4, uncovering novel mechanisms of pathogenesis that extend beyond canonical pathogens5–11. Within this framework, the concept of pathobionts, microorganisms that are typically commensal but acquire pathogenic potential under specific conditions, has emerged as a central theme in chronic airway disease9,11–14.

Bronchiectasis exemplifies this complexity. It is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways, characterized by recurrent infection, het erogeneous clinical presentation, and notable geographic variation. Large-scale microbiome studies implicate both bacteriome and mycobiome composition, interkingdom interactions, host immune responses, and antimicrobial resistance determinants in its pathophysiology15–19. Notably members of the Neisseriaceae, particularly Neisseria subflava, have recently been associated with bronchiectasis in Asian populations13,20–22. Long regarded as a commensal, N. subflava can disrupt epithelial barriers, impair trans-epithelial electrical resistance, and provoke inflammation, thereby driving airway remodelling and immunopathology distinct from established pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa18. Related observations in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) further highlighting the complexity of pathobiont biology and the influence of the environment on their pathogenesis23.

Understanding the commensal-to-pathobiont transition is therefore a critical challenge in microbiology10,18. While Neisseria meningitidis illustrates the devastating potential of such shifts in the upper airway, the mechanisms underlying more transitions in organisms such as N. subflava remain unresolved24–26. Evolutionary pressures within the host, particularly antibiotic exposure, are hypothesized to accelerate adaptation and virulence in commensals, paradoxically, fostering dysbiosis and resistance while treating acute infections10,27,28. Yet, how airway commensals adapt under antibiotic pressure at the genetic and functional levels remains poorly defined29.

Here, we address this knowledge gap by combining experimental evolution with single-bacterial cell transcriptomics to investigate the adaptive responses of N. subflava under ceftriaxone selection. We identify convergent genomic and transcriptional changes involving biofilm maintenance, iron-responsive programs, and cell-wall remodeling that together support increased antibiotic tolerance features consistent with pathogenic potential. By delineating the molecular strategies underlying the commensal-to-pathobiont transition, this work provides new insights into the evolution of the airway microbiome and its implications for chronic respiratory disease.

---

## Results

Experimental evolution of antibiotic resistance and biofilm formation in Neisseria subflava
Neisseria subflava, a commensal of the oral cavity and upper airway, has limited documented antibiotic resistance30,31. To establish a baseline antibiotic susceptibility, we performed dose-response assays using seven antibiotic classes on the clinical isolate SG-KL01 (SG001) obtained from a bronchiectasis patient with a high N. subflava burden18 (Supplementary Fig. 1a-k). Due to the absence of established clinical breakpoints and specific PK/PD parameters for N. subflava, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values served as the primary reference. Initial profiling showed relatively high MIC values (> 0.9 μg/ml) for gentamicin, tetracycline, kanamycin, and ofloxacin, whereas extended-spectrum cephalosporins (ESCs), such as ceftriaxone (Cef) and cefotaxime (CTX), exhibited consistently low MICs, confirming their clinical utility against Neisseriaceae infections (Supplementary Table 1).

Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin widely used in respiratory infections and a key agent in the treatment of Neisseriaceae-associated infections32,33. Despite its broad-spectrum activity, serial ceftriaxone exposure of three independent SG001 lineages (Ca, Cb, Cc) over 26 generations (Fig. 1a) resulted in a 300-fold increase in ceftriaxone MICs (> 5 μg/ml versus 0.02 μg/ml in the parental strain) (Fig. 1b). These evolved lineages also displayed cross-resistance to other β-lactams (ampicillin and penicillin G) while retaining sensitivity to antibiotics outside this class (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 2a-h, Supplementary Table 2), indicating β-lactam-specific resistance development. Concomitantly, all three C26 lineages (C26-a, C26-b, and C26-c) exhibited pronounced colony wrinkling and increased biofilm formation relative to both wild-type and 9th-generation strains (C9-a, C9-b, and C9-c) as confirmed by Congo Red and crystal violet assays (Fig. 1d). Resistance was evident as early as generation 9 (C9-a, C9-b, and C9-c) with MICs of > 0.08 μg/ml in these strains (Supplementary Fig. 2i), suggesting that biofilm development and resistance co-evolve under antibiotic resistance pressure34–36.

Systems-level analysis of ceftriaxone-resistant Neisseria subflava strains
To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying resistance, we performed long-read genome sequencing of evolved strains (Fig. 1e). All assemblies were supported by high coverage and were polished with Illumina short reads, ensuring high confidence in mutation calls. We identified predominant mutations in the ataA gene (QFG95_10090), accounting for 63–77% of the total mutations (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Fig. 2j, Supplementary Data 1). The ataA gene, involved in bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation37, harbored diverse mutational events, including nonsynonymous and synonymous single-nucleotide variations (SNVs), as well as frameshift insertions and deletions. Mutations in other genes, including mltA (QFG95_07970) and QFG95_05805, indicated parallel genomic adaptations under antibiotic pressure.

To confirm independent evolutionary trajectories, we analyzed a SNP-based dendrogram, which supported related but distinct lineages among the replicates (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Because SNPs, especially synonymous ones, can recur under similar selective pressures, we further profiled structural variants (SVs) in C9 lineages using high-resolution long-read sequencing. Large insertions, deletions, duplications, and complex rearrangements were hierarchically clustered by genomic position and variant types, revealing lineage-specific SV patterns unique to each replicate population (C9-a, C9-b, and C9-c) (Supplementary Data 2, Supplementary Fig. 3b-c). Such SV patterns are highly unlikely to arise from parallel evolutionary processes, unlike SNPs, thereby supporting independent evolutionary trajectories and excluding the possibility of cross-contamination among replicates38–40. Consequently, the observed convergence in SNP patterns across the lineages thus likely reflected shared selective pressures rather than technical artifacts.

Phenotypically, resistant strains demonstrated enhanced, rather than impaired, biofilm formation, suggesting the presence of compensatory regulatory pathways beyond ataA mutations. Bulk transcriptomic profiling supported this, revealing upregulation of genes involved in biofilm development, pilus synthesis (comP), iron metabolism (pubB), pyrimidine biosynthesis (pyrDA), carbohydrate metabolism (frk2), and ataA itself in the evolved strain compared to wild-type (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Data 3). Functional gene ontology analyses indicated the coordinated induction of genes involved in cell adhesion and two-component regulatory systems (Supplementary Fig. 2k, Supplementary Data 4), which are essential for biofilm formation and environmental stress responses. Importantly, bulk RNA-seq of the additional evolved lineages (C26-b and C26-c) revealed transcriptional profiles highly consistent with those of C26-a (Supplementary Fig. 3d), reinforcing a common transcriptomic rewiring across independently evolved replicates. Notably, in addition to comP and bamE, several genes that are directly involved in biofilm matrix construction, such as QFG95_07045 (murein-L,D-transpeptidase), murD, milC, murE, and pgpA, were upregulated across resistant lineages. The metal-ion transporter mntB (Mn/Fe uptake) was likewise increased, consistent with enhanced metal homeostasis in the resistant populations. Additionally, enrichment analysis further confirmed convergence on biofilm-formation programs in C26-b and C26-c (Supplementary Fig. 3e). Although the composition of upregulated genes differed across lineages, numerous loci involved in biofilm formation, iron metabolism, and cell-envelope biogenesis were recurrently elevated, albeit with lineage-specific magnitudes. Together with our genomic analyses, these results indicate that sustained antibiotic exposure drives complex adaptive responses in N. subflava, where genomic mutations and transcriptomic rewiring converge to promote antimicrobial resistance. The convergence of biofilm reinforcement and envelope remodeling highlights the plasticity of this commensal species and its capacity to transition toward antibiotic-resistant pathobiont behavior.

Bacterial heterogeneity drives the adaptive evolution of antibiotic resistance in Neisseria subflava
To explore biofilm-related gene expression and functional diversity at single-cell resolution, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on N. subflava cultured under planktonic (shaking) conditions (Fig. 2a). This approach enabled comparison of the transcriptional states of wild-type and ceftriaxone-resistant (C26) strains and highlighted population heterogeneity during antibiotic adaptation. Recent evidence indicates that biofilm and stress-response genes can be activated under planktonic conditions in response to environmental stress or sub-inhibitory antibiotic concentrations, producing a “primed” transcriptional state that precedes biofilm formation41–43. Consistent with this, our data revealed pronounced activation of gene modules associated with antibiotic resistance, with upregulation of biofilm-associated genes in the evolved strain, even under planktonic growth conditions.

We successfully captured single-cell transcriptomes from 9,661 N. subflava cells (3,542 wild-type and 6,119 C26) with comparable sequencing depths across the two groups. Wild-type bacteria averaged 96 ± 126 reads (SD) per cell and expressed 87 ± 43 genes (SD) per cell, while resistant bacteria had similar average reads per cell (194 ± 113) and slightly more genes per cell (95 ± 43) (Supplementary Fig. 4a).

UMAP visualization resolved six transcriptionally distinct populations with differential representation across conditions (Fig. 2b-c, Supplementary Data 5). WT bacteria were enriched in clusters 1 (11.5%), 2 (48.1%), and 3 (34.6%), whereas resistant bacteria primarily occupied clusters 1 (34.7%), 4 (34.4%), 5 (16.3%), and 6 (7.9%). Cluster 1, the most abundant shared population, was characterized by outer membrane porin (porB) and ribosomal genes (rplC, rpsC). Clusters 2 and 3, predominantly found in WT bacteria, were marked by genes involved in RNA processing and protein synthesis (tuf, rhlE), reflecting active growth and metabolic activity. Cluster 3 uniquely expressed lolA, adhesins, and chaperones (dnaK, groL), which play critical roles in outer membrane biogenesis and stress response.

In contrast, resistant-associated clusters exhibited divergent gene expression linked to ceftriaxone resistance. Clusters 4 and 5 shared transcriptional similarities and both upregulated comP (pilin formation), bamE (outer membrane protein assembly), bfrA and bfrB (bacterioferritin linked to oxidative stress mitigation)44, and nirK (a nitrite reductase for detoxification)45. Cluster 5 displayed enhanced metabolic capacity (glyA, acn B, purl, leuS), suggesting an adaptive rewiring of central metabolism to sustain energy demands under antibiotic stress. Lastly, cluster 6 was characterized by sulfur metabolism genes (cysP, cysI, cysJ, cysK), which potentially support alternative redox balance and cell wall modification, enabling evasion of β-lactam targeting.

In concordance with the bulk transcriptomic analysis, scRNA-seq profiling of C26-resistant N. subflava strains revealed key molecular adaptations that confer ceftriaxone resistance, with marked overexpression of comP, bamE, nirK, ataA, as well as carboxymuconolactone decarboxylase family proteins, transferrin-binding proteins and murein-L,D-transpeptidase (Fig. 2d-e, Supplementary Data 6). Although ataA carries a nonsense mutation predicted to produce a truncated, non-functional protein, it nonetheless showed transcriptional upregulation in C26 compared with the WT strain. This suggests a potential compensatory or autoregulatory role in biofilm dysregulation under antibiotic selection. Collectively, these data identify comP and bamE as key genes enriched in resistant-associated clusters, strongly implicating them in biofilm-associated ceftriaxone adaptation.

Lineage-specific functional adaptations for sustaining resistance
Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the cluster-specific marker genes demonstrated that bacterial clusters of the resistant strain possess enhanced oxidoreductase activity, which may neutralize the oxidative stress induced by ceftriaxone while simultaneously activating stress response regulons that promote survival. Interestingly, the peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathways were enriched in clusters 3 and 5, but exhibited divergent genetic programs, with cluster 5 exhibiting important antibiotic adaptations including metal ion binding and enhanced DNA repair capacity, both relevant to countering ceftriaxone-induced damage to cell wall precursors and DNA (Fig. 3a, Supplementary Data 7). KEGG analysis indicated heightened macronutrient metabolism in clusters 4 and 5, supporting the energetic demands of efflux activity and cell-wall repair under cephalosporin pressure (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Data 7). This metabolic rewiring mirrors resistance strategies observed in pathogenic Neisseria species, where increased metabolic flux through the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation supports β-lactam resistance46. The specialized functions of clusters 4 and 5, particularly their overexpression of denitrification genes (nirK, ncd2, norB), competence and adherence factors (comP, bamE), SOS and stress response (sodB, cspA, rnr, recQ), and metal ion acquisition systems (bfrA, bfrB, lutA1, pqqL), collectively reinforce envelope integrity, limit oxidative damage, and maintain metal homeostasis under ceftriaxone exposure (Fig. 3c). By contrast, cluster 6 adopted a metabolically conservative program characterized by sulfate assimilation (cysP, cysI, cysJ, cysK), redox activity (nuoF, nuoD, nqrB) and selected efflux transporters (tet(M), acrB, potA, tet35) (Fig. 3b-c). As sulfate assimilation precedes cysteine biosynthesis, this transcriptional profile indicates elevated cysteine production to bolster redox balance and antioxidant defenses during β-lactam-induced envelope stress.

Although bfrA and bfrB genes primarily function as iron-storage proteins, they may secondarily contribute to enhancing biofilm stability and stress tolerance47–49. Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) confirmed increased intracellular Fe levels in resistant versus wild-type bacteria, consistent with elevated expression of iron-related genes, while Mg levels remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 4b). We also compared the growth kinetics of wild-type and C26 strains. The C26 strain also showed accelerated growth rates and higher stationary-phase density, consistent with enhanced metabolism and proliferative potential (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Additionally, we established a bfrSA-gfp genomic reporter system to directly assess iron-dependent gene regulation. Upon iron supplementation (50 μM FeCl₃), we observed robust induction of GFP fluorescence driven by the bfrA promoter, confirming enhanced iron-responsive gene activity in the evolved C26 strain (Supplementary Fig. 4d). These results provide direct support for the adaptive role of metal homeostasis identified by single-cell analyses, reinforcing the crucial role of iron regulation in cephalosporin resistance.

Among these modules, comP and bamE showed peak expression in the resistance-associated cluster 5, highlighting their central roles within the dominant adaptive lineage and linking biofilm features with antibiotic tolerance. To assess whether planktonic culture conditions could obscure biofilm-specific expression, RT-qPCR was performed under both planktonic (shaking) and sessile (biofilm-promoting) conditions. The evolved C26 strain maintained similarly elevated expression of both genes under planktonic and sessile conditions, whereas wild-type cells showed no significant difference (Supplementary Fig. 4e). Thus, the resistant lineage maintains a constitutively “primed” biofilm transcriptome across growth modes. At the population level, comP and bamE are the principal genetic drivers linking biofilm enhancement to ceftriaxone resistance. ComP encodes a DNA uptake minor pilin that mediates natural competence and facilitates incorporation of extracellular DNA (eDNA) into the matrix, a structural component that reinforces Neisseria biofilms and stabilizes surface communities under antibiotic stress50–52. BamE, a lipoprotein of the β-barrel assembly machinery (BAM), ensures efficient outer-membrane protein assembly, preserving the integrity and architecture of the biofilm surface layer and reducing β-lactam permeability53–55. Together, comP-driven eDNA enrichment and bamE-mediated envelope stabilization establish a biofilm phenotype that shields cells from cephalosporin penetration and maintains a microenvironment conducive to horizontal gene exchange.

Single-cell RNA-seq revealed functional heterogeneity underpinning ceftriaxone resistance in N. subflava, which confers a survival advantage by enabling specialized roles, enhancing resilience, and supporting long-term adaptation29,56. This resistance is centred on a biofilm-oriented programme driven by comP-mediated extracellular DNA enrichment and bamE-dependent outer-membrane stabilisation. This programme converges with the functional enrichment profiles of clusters 4-6, where stress-response activation, cell-wall remodelling and metal-ion homeostasis form an integrated network that maintains biofilm integrity under sustained β-lactam pressure. These findings support a model in which resistance evolution is intrinsically linked to biofilm optimisation, providing immediate protection from antibiotic challenge while preserving a genetic reservoir for long-term adaptation.

Elevated expression of comP and bamE drives antibiotic resistance and immune evasion
Building on these observations, we next dissected the functional contributions of comP and bamE as the principal biofilm-linked drivers, alongside bfrA and bfrB as bacterioferritin-associated iron homeostasis modules. To assess gene expression at single‑cell resolution, we integrated chromosomally integrated fluorescent reporters (mCherry for comP and GFP for bamE) in both wild-type and C26 strains. Fluorescence microscopy revealed markedly increased reporter intensity in the evolved C26 strain, with a larger fraction of cells showing high comP and bamE expression compared with the wild type (Fig. 4a).

MIC assays confirmed that the overexpression of comP and bamE enhanced ceftriaxone resistance, with MIC values of 0.2 μg/ml and 0.1 μg/ml, respectively, representing a 5-10-fold increase compared to vector controls. Conversely, deletion of comP or bamE reduced MICs by approximately two-fold, confirming their essential roles in resistance (Fig. 4b). Both genes also promoted biofilm maturation. Their overexpression enhanced biofilm mass, whereas deletion markedly impaired biofilm formation (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 5a). Overexpression of bfrA and bfrB did not affect ceftriaxone resistance and had a minor impact on biofilm mass, suggesting their limited role. Macrophage phagocytosis assays revealed enhanced resistance to phagocytic clearance in strains overexpressing comP and bamE, consistent with their roles in biofilm formation and immune evasion (Fig. 4d).

The clinical relevance of these findings was supported by analysis of patient cohorts. In bronchiectasis patients from Shenzhen, China, N. subflava was detected in 18.4% of samples (n = 38) (Supplementary Fig. 5c), with carriers generally being older and showing lower leukocyte counts (Supplementary Fig. 5d). In an independent cohort, nine clinical isolates were examined by multilocus sequence typing (MLST), which grouped them into three sequence types: ST-a (n = 6), ST-b (n = 1), and ST-c (n = 2). ST-a isolates exhibited significant upregulation of comP and bamE, which correlated with enhanced biofilm formation and higher ceftriaxone MICs (Fig. 4e-f; Supplementary Fig. 5b). Whole-genome sequencing further revealed frequent ataA mutations across clinical isolates, particularly in ST-a isolates, suggesting that comP and bamE upregulation may compensate for impaired ataA function. This suggests comP and bamE upregulation potentially compensates for impaired ataA function, promoting adaptation under antibiotic pressure. Consistent with this, ST-a isolates formed more robust biofilms than ST-b or ST-c strains, mirroring the phenotypes observed in experimentally evolved resistant lineages (Fig. 4g).

Taken together, our results demonstrate direct involvement of comP and bamE in ceftriaxone resistance, biofilm formation, and immune evasion in N. subflava. By contrast, iron-storage genes bfrA and bfrB play ancillary roles in this emerging pathobiont.

Iron enhances biofilm formation and antibiotic resistance in ceftriaxone-evolved N. subflava
Although the precise roles of bfrA and bfrB were not resolved functionally, their upregulation in C26 antibiotic-resistant strains suggests that iron homeostasis could modulate adaptation under antibiotic stress. We therefore examined the effect of iron (Fe³⁺) supplementation on bacterial survival and biofilm formation in wild-type (WT) and ceftriaxone-resistant (C26) strains.

In colony-forming unit (CFU) assays, Fe³⁺ supplementation did not alter the viability of wild-type strain at its MIC (0.02 μg/ml) but markedly improved survival of the C26 strain at its higher MIC (6 µg/ml) (Fig. 5a). Fe³⁺ supplementation had no impact on WT viability at its MIC (0.02 μg/ml), indicating iron availability does not influence WT growth at low antibiotic pressure. In contrast, Fe³⁺ markedly enhanced viability of the C26 strain at its higher MIC (6 μg/ml), significantly reducing ceftriaxone susceptibility. In the absence of iron supplementation, the viability of the C26 strain sharply declined, underscoring the critical role of iron in sustaining resistance under antibiotic exposure (Fig. 5b).

Biofilm formation showed that Fe³⁺ supplementation increased biofilm biomass in both strains under antibiotic-free conditions, with the evolved C26 strain exhibiting greater biofilm formation compared to WT. Under ceftriaxone treatment at MIC levels, biofilm biomass in the WT strain remained unaffected by iron supplementation, whereas the C26 strain showed significantly increased biofilm biomass, indicative of reduced antibiotic susceptibility (Fig. 5c-d).

Further assessment of bacterial survival across a gradient of antibiotic pressures highlighted strain-specific advantages provided by Fe³⁺ supplementation. At ceftriaxone concentrations slightly above WT MIC (0.02–0.04 μg/ml), WT viability was minimal, irrespective of iron availability. In contrast, Fe³⁺ supplementation substantially enhanced the viability of the C26 strain even at higher ceftriaxone concentrations (6-8 μg/ml), further confirming iron’s role in resistance under significant antibiotic stress (Fig. 5e-f).

These findings highlight iron’s dual contribution to biofilm formation and bacterial viability under antibiotic challenge, specifically benefiting the evolved, resistant C26 strain. Although iron broadly supports biofilm development, only the antibiotic-adapted strain effectively utilizes iron-enhanced biofilms to sustain ceftriaxone tolerance. This highlights ceftriaxone resistance as a modifiable trait in antibiotic-adapted N. subflava, influenced by iron availability via supplementation or chelation.

## Methods

All experiments were performed using standard microbiological techniques unless otherwise specified. A complete list of bacterial strains, plasmids, and reagents used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Ethics statement
The study involving human clinical samples was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Shenzhen Third People's Hospital (Ethics approval number: 2024-153). Informed consent was obtained from all participants involved in the study.

Bacterial culture media
Neisseria subflava was initially recovered from glycerol stocks stored at -80°C and cultured on Columbia blood agar plates (Columbia agar supplemented with 5% defibrinated sheep blood) at 37 °C in a 5% CO₂ incubator for 14 h. Subsequently, a single colony was transferred to Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) liquid medium (Cat#024053, HKM, China) supplemented with 5% fetal bovine serum (FBS)for culture. Bacteria were incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO₂ incubator for an additional 12–16 h to ensure optimal growth.

MIC determination (Minimum Inhibitory Concentration)
The overnight bacterial cultures were re-inoculated at a 1:1000 dilution into fresh medium and allowed to grow to the mid-log phase in a shaking incubator (cat#MQT-60R, Minquan, China) at 37 °C, 220 rpm. The bacterial solution was added to a transparent 96-well plate at a final concentration of OD 0.01 per well, and a gradient dilution of antibiotic concentration using BHI, 600 with four parallels for each concentration. After culturing the bacteria in various concentrations of antibiotics for 24 h, the absorbance at 600 nm was measured to determine the antibacterial effect. Fitting curves by comparing different concentrations of antibiotics and absorbance to obtain IC90 (Inhibitory Concentration 90). Use GraphPad Prism 8 (GraphPad Software) to calculate S-type dose response (slope variation) nonlinear fitting.

Biofilm formation assay
Overnight cultures were diluted to OD of 0.01 and the 96-well plates were cultured at 37 °C for 600 24 h, then cell plates were washed three times with PBS to remove unbound bacteria. Then biofilm was evaluated by 0.05% crystal violet (CV: 150 μl; Sangon Biotech, China) staining for 30 minutes84. Gently rinsed unbound dyes with sterile dd H O and blown dried at room temperature. 2 After that, 200 μl of 30% glacial acetic acid was added to each well. Relative biofilm formation was determined by measuring the absorbance at 550 nm with Tecan Infinity 200 PRO microplate reader. Biofilm inhibition experiments were conducted in three independent trials, with four replicates per condition.

Congo red plate assay
Columbia agar was autoclaved, cooled to 50-55 °C, mixed with 5% sterile defibrinated sheep blood, supplemented with 10 μg/mL Coomassie brilliant blue G-250 and 20 μg/mL Congo red (CR), and poured into plates to solidify. Fresh overnight bacterial culture (5 μl per spot, 5 replicates) was spotted onto the plates, which were incubated at room temperature in the dark for 72 h, and then colony staining characteristics were observed and recorded.

Growth curve assay
To assess growth kinetics of wild-type and evolved isolates, overnight cultures were initially adjusted to an OD₆₀₀ 1.0 in BTHI broth. The standardized suspensions were diluted into fresh BHI medium supplemented with 5% FBS to a starting OD₆₀₀ of approximately 0.02. Aliquots of 200 μl were transferred to flat-bottom 96-well microtiter plates (Corning), with at least three technical replicates per strain. Plates were incubated at 37 °C in TECAN Spark microplate reader, which recorded OD₆₀₀ every 30 minutes for 48 hours with continuous double orbital shaking between reads. Blank wells containing medium only were included for background correction. Growth curves were plotted and analyzed using GraphPad Prism 8. Parameters including lag phase duration, exponential growth rate, and maximal OD were extracted to compare relative growth 600 fitness between strains.

Preprocessing for single-cell sequencing
Wild-type and antibiotic-resistant strains were cultured at 37 °C with shaking at 220 rpm. Cultures were grown for approximately 6 hours until the optical density at 600 nm (OD ) reached 1.0. To 600 minimize technical artifacts and preserve in vivo transcriptomic states, all subsequent steps were performed on ice (4 °C), and all buffers were pre-chilled. The time from harvest to fixation was strictly limited to under 10 minutes for all samples. Wild-type and C26 strains were processed in parallel under identical conditions to ensure comparability. 1 ml of each bacterial culture was collected and centrifuged at 6,010 × g for 5 minutes. The supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was washed with 1 ml of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The washed bacterial pellet was resuspended in 1 ml of ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS. The suspension was placed in a rotary mixer at 4 °C and rotated for 9 hours to cross-link intracellular RNA, DNA, and proteins. After fixation, the samples were centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 10 minutes at 4 °C to remove the PFA. The pellet was washed twice with 1 ml of PBS-T (PBS containing 0.1% Tween-20 and 1 µl RNAse inhibitor). The bacterial pellet was then resuspended in 200 µl of PBS-T, with an additional 5 µl of RNAse inhibitor added. The tubes were sealed and stored at 4 °C until further use. Prior to single-cell sequencing, quality control of the samples was performed to ensure a cell count of ≥ 10 million, minimal debris, no visible clumping, and an aggregation rate of ≤ 20%.

Single-cell RNA sequencing
Single-cell encapsulation, droplet generation, and nucleic acid capture were conducted using the VITAcruizer DP400 instrument (Cat#E20000131, M20 Genomics), following the VITApilote High-Throughput Single-Bacterial Transcriptome Kit protocol (Cat#R20114124, M20 Genomics). Fixed bacterial cells underwent permeabilization and cell wall digestion, followed by reverse transcription with random primers to produce full-length cDNA. After adaptor ligation, cell barcodes and unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) on microbeads were combined with adaptor-ligated cDNA and encapsulated in droplets. Droplet encapsulation and extension generated labeled cDNA, which was then PCR-amplified. The final library, incorporating P5 and P7 adaptors, was sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform.

Single-cell data preprocessing
Single-cell RNA sequencing data were processed using VITAseer V1.2 software (M20 Genomics), designed specifically for transcriptomic data generated by the VITA platform. Briefly, raw sequencing reads were trimmed using Cutadapt (Pv3.7). For each Read1, unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and cell-specific barcodes were extracted, with acceptable barcodes defined as those with a Hamming distance ≤ 2 nt and a unique match. Read2 was aligned to the reference genome of the species of interest using STAR (v2.7.10a) under default parameters, retaining only uniquely mapped sequences for downstream analysis. Subsequent data analysis was performed using Seurat (v4.3.0.1) under default parameters unless specified otherwise. Cells expressing fewer than 10 genes were excluded, and genes present in fewer than one cell were filtered out. Data were log-normalized using NormalizeData function, followed by FindVariableFeatures function to identify highly variable features for dimensional reduction. The data were scaled with ScaleData function. Dimension reduction was performed by principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensions to 8. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) was constructed using these principal components. Clustering was performed using the Louvain algorithm (FindClusters) at a resolution of 0.5, and differential gene expression was assessed with a log-fold change threshold of 0.25 and adjusted p-value of < 0.05 (FindMarkers function).

GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of DEGs
Based on the hypergeometric tests, GO and KEGG enrichment analysis of DEGs was performed to identify the significantly enriched terms using clusterProfiler package (v4. 16.0) in R (v4.5.1).

Genomic DNA extraction and genome sequencing
Neisseria subflava SG-KL01 (SG001) were grown to 109 CFU/ml, and total DNA was extracted from each 2 ml bacterial suspension using the TIANamp Bacterial DNA Kit (Tiangen Biotech, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Qualified genomic DNA was fragmented with G-tubes (Covaris, Woburn, MA, USA), followed by end-repair using the NEBNext FFPE DNA Repair Kit (M6630, NEB, USA) and NEBNext End Repair/dA-Tailing Module reagents (E7546, NEB, USA). The fragmented DNA was subsequently ligated to adapters to construct sequencing libraries using NEBNext Quick Ligation Module reagents (E6056, NEB, USA). After purification with the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA), library sequencing was performed on the Oxford Nanopore PromethION long-read sequencing platform (Oxford Nanopore Technologies, Oxford, UK) following standard protocols. For Illumina sequencing, qualified genomic DNA was first randomly sonicated, then subjected to end-repair, A-tailing, and adapter ligation using the NEBNext® Ultra™ DNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA fragments of 300-400 bp (in length) were enriched by PCR. Finally, PCR products were purified using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA). Library size distribution was analyzed with the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent, Santa Clara, CA), and quantification was performed by real-time PCR. Genome sequencing was conducted on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform using paired-end technology (PE150).

Genome assembly and quality control
Raw ONT (.fast5) signals were base-called with Oxford Nanopore Guppy v6.4.6 (HAC), followed by quality control to remove reads with Q < 7 and trim adapter-containing reads, and the filtered data were used for assembly and alignment. Raw Illumina reads were processed with FASTP v0.20.0 to (i) remove adapters (trimming adapters and downstream sequence; reads < 50 nt after trimming were discarded), (ii) remove poly-A reads, (iii) remove reads with N > 10%, and (iv) remove low-quality reads where Q ≤ 20 bases constituted ≥ 50% of the read; the resulting clean reads were aligned to the assembly with BWA v0.7.17-r1188 and used for iterative polishing with Pilon v1.23 to obtain the final genome sequence. Per-base coverage was obtained with samtools depth (v1.16.1; ONT) and bedtools genomecov (v2.30.0; Illumina), and coverage breadth at thresholds (≥1×–≥200×) was derived from these per-base depths (Supplementary Data 8). Inter-assembly variant calling was performed by whole-genome alignment with MUMmer v3.1 and regional structural variation interpreted with SyRI v1.4; SNPs/indels were derived from MUMmer/nucmer alignments (parameters: --maxmatch -c 100 -b 200 -l 50), and SVs were detected with SyRI (parameters: --unic 100 -k).

Bulk RNA-seq library preparation, sequencing and analysis
For RNA extraction, overnight cultures of SG001 were diluted to an optical density (OD) at 600 nm of 0.01 and grown at 37 °C with shaking at 220 rpm for 12 h. Total RNA was extracted from whole cells with EASYspin Plus Bacterial RNA Rapid Extraction Kit (cat#RN43, Aidlab, China), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA purity and quantity were evaluated using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). RNA integrity was assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). After rRNA depletion, RNA was fragmented in fragmentation buffer and subjected to first- and second-strand cDNA synthesis, followed by end repair, A-tailing and adaptor ligation (with USER treatment where applicable). Libraries were PCR-amplified, purified with AMPure XP beads, and size-selected to 370-420 bp prior to final QC. Qualified libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 to generate 150-bp paired-end (PE150) reads. Adapters and low-quality bases were trimmed with cutadapt; reads < 50 nt or with > 10% N were discarded, and reads mapping to rRNA were removed to obtain clean reads. Per-sample metrics (Raw reads, Adapter trimmed, rRNA removed, Clean rate, Q20/Q30, GC%) were summarised. Clean reads were aligned to the Neisseria subflava reference genome using STAR (default parameters), retaining uniquely mapped reads. Gene-level raw counts were obtained with featureCountsR; TPM values were additionally computed for display/visualisation only and were not used for statistical testing. Differential expression was performed on raw counts using edgeR (negative-binomial modelling with multiple-testing correction); unless otherwise specified, genes with p < 0.05 and |log fold change| ≥ 1 were considered differentially expressed, and FDR values were reported. For visualisation, the TPM matrix of DEGs was transformed as log (TPM + 1), row-wise Z-scored, and subjected to hierarchical clustering of genes and samples to generate heatmaps. 2

Bacterial strains and genomic sequencing
The clinical isolate Neisseria subflava strains (SG001–009) were isolated from patients with bronchiectasis or other chronic lung diseases in the Singapore-Kuala Lumpur region (SG-KL, Malaysia)18. Genomic DNA was extracted from overnight cultures using the TIANamp Bacteria DNA Kit (cat#GDP302-02, Tiangen, China) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. High-throughput sequencing was conducted on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, generating paired-end reads with a read length of 150 bp. Raw sequencing reads were assessed for quality using FastQC (version 0.11.9) and subsequently trimmed using Trimmomatic (version 0.39) to remove low-quality bases and adapter sequences. De novo genome assembly was performed using SPAdes (v3.15.4) under default settings, and genome annotations were generated using Prokka (v1.14.6).

ICP-MS analysis of intracellular metal content
Bacterial cultures of wild-type and evolved (C26) Neisseria subflava strains were grown to mid-log phase in BHI broth at 37 °C with shaking. Approximately 1 × 10⁹ colony-forming units (CFU) were harvested by centrifugation at 5,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. Washed pellets were resuspended in 200 μl of ultrapure water and subjected to acid digestion by adding 500 μl of 65% trace-metal-grade nitric acid (HNO₃) in metal-free Teflon tubes. Digestion was carried out at 95 °C for 1 hour in a closed heating block or using a microwave digestion system where available, following validated protocols for biological samples. After cooling to room temperature, the digests were diluted to 5 ml with ultrapure water and filtered through a 0.22 μm PTFE filter to remove particulates. Metal ion concentrations (Fe, Mg) were quantified by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS, Agilent 7900) under standard operating conditions with helium collision mode. Calibration was performed using certified multi-element standards. Three biological replicates were analyzed for each strain.

RAW264.7 cell phagocytosis resistance assay
RAW264.7 murine macrophage-like cells were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂. Cells were seeded at a density of 5 × 10⁵ cells per well in 12-well plates and incubated overnight to allow adhesion. Neisseria subflava strains were grown overnight in BHI medium at 37 °C with shaking. Cultures were diluted to an OD600 of 0.6 in fresh BHI medium and grown to mid-log phase. Bacterial cells were washed twice with PBS, resuspended in antibiotic-free DMEM, and added to the RAW264.7 cells at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 100:1. Plates were centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 minutes to synchronize infection and then incubated for 1 hour at 37 °C with 5% CO₂. Following infection, cells were treated with 100 µg/mL gentamicin for 30 min at 37 °C to eliminate extracellular bacteria after PBS washing, then washed again and lysed with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS. The lysates were serially diluted. Dilutions were plated on BHI agar and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h to determine colony-forming units (CFU). CFU counts were normalized to the initial RAW264.7 cell density, and results were expressed as mean ± SD from three independent experiments.

Sequence typing (ST) analysis
Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) was conducted using the MLST scheme for Neisseria species. Seven housekeeping genes (abcZ, adk, aroE, fumC, gdh, pdhC, and pgm) were amplified and aligned against the PubMLST database. The resulting ST profiles were clustered using goeBURST to determine phylogenetic relationships. SG001–006 were assigned to the ST-a group, SG007 was classified as the ST-b group, and SG008 and SG009 were grouped into the ST-c group.

RT-qPCR
Total RNA was extracted using EASYspin Plus Bacterial RNA Rapid Extraction Kit, (cat#RN43, Aidlab, China). RNA concentrations were measured using NanoDrop 2000c (Thermo Fisher, USA) and normalized among the experimental sample set. cDNA was reverse transcribed using the PrimeScriptTM RT reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (TaKaRa Bio, Japan) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The SYBR Green Pro Taq HS qPCR Premix (Cat#AG11701, AG, China) and reactions were run on ABI Step One Plus Real-Time PCR equipment in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). The levels of target genes were normalized to the levels of gene actin (Gyrb) mRNA and relative expression was determined according to the ΔΔCt method. Three candidate genes (comP, bamE, bfrA, and bfrB) were randomly selected from the transcriptome data to verify the accuracy of the transcriptome data; the primers are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Gene Knockout in Neisseria subflava
Approximately 700 bp sequences flanking the upstream and downstream regions of the target gene were PCR-amplified from N. subflava genomic DNA, using primers listed in Supplementary Table 7. The gentamicin resistance cassette, containing its own promoter and terminator, was PCR-amplified from a plasmid template. These three fragments (upstream arm, gentamicin cassette, downstream arm) were fused into a single linear knockout cassette by overlap extension PCR and verified by agarose gel electrophoresis. For transformation, N. subflava was streaked on blood agar plates and incubated overnight at 37 °C. Fresh colonies were scraped and resuspended in ice-cold 0.3 M sucrose, washed three times, and finally resuspended in 0.3 M sucrose to adjust the suspension to an OD600 of approximately 1.5. Fifty microliters of electrocompetent cells were mixed with ~1 µg of purified knockout cassette and transferred into a pre-chilled 0.2 cm electroporation cuvette. Electroporation was performed using a Bio-Rad Gene Pulser at 2.5 kV, and cells were immediately recovered in 1 ml of pre-warmed BHI broth with 15% FBS at 37 °C with gentle shaking (110 rpm) for 2-6 h. Transformants were selected on blood agar supplemented with 15 µg/ml gentamicin and incubated at 37 °C for 36-48 h. Gentamicin-resistant colonies were screened by PCR using primers flanking the homologous arms, and correct gene replacement was further confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Colonies were screened by colony PCR with primers outside the homologous regions, and positive mutants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

Fluorescent Tagging via Homologous Recombination
For in situ fluorescent tagging (comP::mCherry, bamE::gfp, and bfrA::gfp), the double-crossover homologous recombination strategy described above was employed, with the fluorescent marker gene (mCherry or gfp) inserted in-frame at the target locus along with a gentamicin resistance cassette for selection. Fusion constructs consisted of relatively long homologous arms flanking the target site, along with external primers to enhance transformation efficiency. Electroporation, recovery, and selection were performed as described for gene knockout mutants. Correctly tagged clones were verified by fluorescence microscopy, PCR, and Sanger sequencing. Strains were cultured overnight on blood agar, then inoculated into BHI broth and grown at 37 °C with shaking (220 rpm) to mid-log phase (OD600 ≈ 0.5-0.8). Bacterial cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed once with PBS, and resuspended in PBS. A 5 μl aliquot was spotted onto a glass slide for microscopy. In bacterial live-cell localization experiments, the ECLIPSE Ti2-I microscope was used to capture both mCherry and GFP channel fluorescence, as well as bright-field images of bacteria. NIS-Elements Viewer 5.27 was employed for subsequent image processing. For each condition, three independent fields of view were analyzed. Primers for fluorescent reporter fusions (comP::mCherry, bamE::gfp, bfrA::gfp) are provided in Supplementary Table 6.

Fluorescence Imaging of bfrA::gfp
To assess iron-dependent expression of the bfrA::gfp reporter, single colonies were inoculated from blood agar into BHI broth and cultured at 37 °C with shaking (220 rpm) to mid-log phase (OD600 ≈ 0.5-0.8). Cultures were divided and supplemented with FeCl₃ (0 or 50 μM final concentration), followed by continued incubation for 6 hours. Bacterial cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed with PBS, and resuspended in PBS. A 5 μl aliquot was placed on a glass slide for microscopy. The ECLIPSE Ti2-I microscope was used to capture fluorescent images of bacteria, and NIS-Elements Viewer 5.27 was employed for subsequent image processing. Three independent fields of view were analyzed per group.

Cloning procedures and overexpression of genes
DNA cloning and plasmid construction were performed using standard molecular biology techniques. PCR primers were designed to incorporate BamHI and HindIII restriction sites at their 5’ ends, enabling the subsequent digestion and ligation of the target gene into the pMCS5 vector, which harbors a tetracycline resistance gene. Seamless cloning was performed according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. The recombinant plasmid was introduced into Escherichia coli DH5α and Neisseria subflava via electroporation. Positive clones were selected on 5% sheep blood agar plates supplemented with 15 µg/ml tetracycline (TC), and all plasmids were verified by Sanger sequencing. Neisseria subflava strains harboring the recombinant plasmid were cultured in medium containing 15 µg/ml TC until reaching logarithmic growth, at which point gene expression was induced with 1 mM IPTG. The overexpressed gene is in Supplementary Table 5.

Bacterial isolation from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF)
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples were collected from 38 patients with bronchiectasis undergoing fiberoptic bronchoscopy at Shenzhen Third People's Hospital, based on clinical indications. During the procedure, sterile 0.9% saline was instilled into the right middle lobe or lingular segment of the bronchus and recovered using low-pressure suction (≤ 100 mmHg). Samples were immediately placed on ice to preserve microbiome composition, then centrifuged at 3,000 × g, 4 °C for 10 min, and the pellet was resuspended in sterile PBS. To maximize bacterial recovery, aliquots were plated onto chocolate agar and sheep blood agar (37 °C, 5% CO₂, 48 h) for common respiratory pathogens, MacConkey agar (37 °C, aerobic incubation, 48 h) for Gram-negative bacteria, and CDC anaerobic agar (37 °C, anaerobic conditions, 5-7 days) for anaerobic species. After single-colony purification, individual bacterial isolates were selected for species identification using 16S rRNA sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

Statistical analyses
All data analysis was expressed as the mean ± SD. Each experiment was repeated a minimum of three times, with statistical analysis based on biological replicates. Detailed information regarding replicates and statistical methods for each experiment can be found in the figure legends and the Source data file. Differences were considered significant when the P value was < 0.05. GraphPad Prism 8 software (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) was used to analyze the experimental data.

Data availability
These datasets are publicly accessible and provide detailed information to support data validation, reproducibility, and further analysis by the research community. The transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing datasets generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA). The single-cell RNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq datasets for wild-type and C26-a strains are available under BioProject accession PRJNA1209901, and the whole-genome sequencing data are under PRJNA1208745. To support lineage-level validation, additional bulk RNA-seq datasets for independently evolved C26-b and C26-c strains have been deposited under BioProject accession PRJNA1292455. All data are publicly available as of the date of publication. Source Data are provided with this paper.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript “Single-bacterial cell insights into mechanisms of ceftriaxone resistance in Neisseria subflava” presents a
multifaceted study that aims to understand mechanisms of evolved resistance to antibiotics by Neisseria subflava. This
bacterium has recently been implicated with airway disease and presents a unique way to track genetic changes that allow
organisms typically existing as commensals to become pathogenic. In this study the authors use a lab-based evolution
approach to evolve Neisseria in the presence of a relevant antibiotic in order to identify genetic changes that are
accumulated. Triplicate cultures are used to try and uncover mutations that are repeated and are therefore deterministic. The
study then checks whether evolved strains have resistance to multiple antibiotics and attempts to characterize the
mechanisms of resistance. This characterization is first done using physiological measurements that demonstrate that the
evolved cultures have greater biofilm producing capacity despite all cultures having mutation that inactivate a key biofilm
regulator. Then the authors use traditional bulk RNAseq analysis to identify gene expression changes differentiating one of
the lineages from the parental strain. After this analysis the authors use a bacterial single cell sequencing approach to try
and understand the behavior of the culture. This single cell RNAseq characterization is the section of the manuscript that is
used to make many of the less substantiated and more bold claims but unfortunately this section has several major issues
with study design, analysis and interpretation. Importantly, the author's central claim is that the core mechanism of resistance
is through biofilm formation, but the single cell analysis is all done on planktonic cultures grown with much shaking. In
addition, the authors point to varied states and trajectories that are supposed to be different between the parent strain and
evolved culture (which apparently was only done for one of the lineages) - but the changes appear to be minimal and the
trajectory analysis, which is notoriously a non-reliable single cell analysis method even in higher organisms that have
defined developmental processes, is not validated by any dynamic measurement and makes several assumptions that are
not founded. Furthermore, data that is critical to assess the quality and interpretation of the results is missing and primary
data is not present in the manuscript, supplementary figures or supplementary tables, which make it impossible to
understand how conclusions are drawn. After the single cell analysis the authors use a genetic approach to try and validate
a few of the findings, focusing on biofilm-associated genes comP and bamE and iron-acquisition related genes bfrA and bfrB
from mutagenesis and the RNAseq data, but this approach too has some weaknesses. Overall the manuscript presented
here used many techniques and boldly attempted to provide a comprehensive look at evolution of a pathobiont, but in its
current form it is missing too much pertinent information and contains several critical shortcomings that need to be
addressed. There are many technical concerns which kept my revision to the most important major points, but there are also
numerous small mistakes in figures and text that would need to be addressed.
Major points:
1) Section on lab-based evolution and phenotypic (biofilm) characterization:
a. Three replicates were used for the evolution, in keeping with standard practices in lab-based evolution to compare
evolved trajectories in several parallel cultures but in most studies more than 3 are used (6 or 10 are current standards). Is
there a reason 3 was chosen? Also, the mutational signatures between replicates looks eerily similar in supplementary
figure 2J, are there any measures taken to make sure that no cross contamination occurred? Often times looking at repeated
synonymous mutations can identify whether this is an issue
b. The authors refer to their evolution approach throughout the manuscript as “Directed Evolution” – a term that is used for
molecular evolution strategies used very differently than in the current manuscript to enhance activity of enzymes by
focusing on distinct parts of a functional gene for specific improvement. What they do to here is “lab-based evolution”. This
may sound like a semantic distinction but it is a very important difference as these are two highly distinct fields.
c. There is critical information missing about the mutational analysis. The methods section does not actually discuss how
long reads were processed, what read coverage was and how similar mutations were called – these are all needed to
understand what was done and the quality of the data and require a methods section – especially dealing with long read
sequencing which (*using some platforms at least*) can have lower fidelity
d. In initial characterization of biofilms all the data shown is from one replicate, it is important to see how different the
replicates are from each other.
2) Section on traditional RNAseq transcriptomics:
a. The traditional RNAseq it appears triplicates were used (though this is not mentioned in the methods but there are 3
columns in the figure for wildtype and the evolved strain). One question is which of the evolved strains was used and why all
evolved strains were not tested?
b. Gene enrichments are provided but no statistics are given and the list of genes used to define each category in the
geneset enrichment is not given. These are needed to determine what each gene set actually represents.
3) Section on Single Cell RNAseq
a. A major flaw in logic from the first sections to single cell and bulk transcriptomics is that the authors hypothesize that
biofilm is important for antibiotic survival in the evolved strains, but both bulk and single cell transcriptomics were done with
planktonic cultures grown for only a few hours with high speed shaking, conditions that are not particularly suitable for
biofilms.
b. The authors need to provide any statistics about the scRNAseq data quality (for example reads per cell, genes captured
per cell, etc).
c. The authors need to provide supplemental information with the differentially expressed genes in each cluster. For now
there is a heatmap but this does not provide pertinent information like P-values, log change, and genes beyond the selected
few genes per cluster.
d. The authors make a claim that the difference in abundance in the evolved strain for the “metal binding cluster” are different
– but in reality a change from 16.6% cells to 19.5% cells in a couple of replicates *(not clear how many if any replicates are
used) does not seem statistically significant, and even if it is statistically significant biologically this would not likely be
significant.
e. Overall the UMAP of the wildtype and evolved strains look strikingly similar (as close to identical as I could imagine single
cell data looking) – this makes it hard to claim that these are truly distinct.
f. The authors ascribe biological function to clusters (“proliferating”, “iron scavenging” etc) – these cannot be made just
based on transcriptomic data, the authors need to validate these with physiological measurements. This is especially true for
any definitions that rely on growth rates etc.
g. Technique wise there is concern about the transcriptomic data because cells were processed for at least 10 minutes
before fixation – bacterial mRNA half life is on the order of 1-2 minutes so many changes can be due to adaptation to PBS,

h. The scRNAseq only compared wildtype to one of the 3 lineages in evolution, and not all 3, yet authors want to draw
conclusions about general mechanisms of evolution. At the very least they need to change the language to explain that this
may not be a general result
i. The pseudotime analysis relies entirely on a pipeline (Monocle2) that was developed for mammalian systems and often
provides erroneous temporal projections. Pseudotime analysis needs to be validated with timelapse or other kinetic
measurements of gene expression that show that the proposed trajectories are actually meaningful. In bacterial transcription the
activation of genes is often pulsatile and there is no way to know if pulses are coordinated over time without dynamic
measurements.
j. The pseudotime comparison of the Wildtype and evolved lineage leave many questions about underlying data quality and
the analysis commands used, without seeing the actual pseudotime trajectory maps themselves it is hard for a reviewer to
judge if the data is actually reasonable. In the limited data presented a troubling aspect is that there are duplicates of porB.
Unfortunately none of the monocle steps or QC outputs (from Monocle or the other single cell analyses) are included in the
supplementary and the methods do not provide needed information to understand the data quality and exactly what was
done.
4) Sections on Genetic Follow Up
a. The authors use plasmid-based fluorescent reporters, ideally chromosomal integration would be used to show
heterogeneity and not plasmids.
b. The differences seen in qPCR (figure 4e) appear to be statistically significant but it is not at all clear if such a small fold-
wise effect (less than 2-fold) would actually have biological meaning.
c. To show involvement of comP and bamE they were overexpressed with a strong promoter, it would be nice to see the
effect of deletion or a weaker promoter.

We clarify emphasize that the pronounced transcriptional heterogeneity and emergence
of distinct lineages observed in our evolved populations are not experimental artifacts, but
reflect fundamental adaptive strategies. Despite rigorous efforts to standardize experimental
conditions, we consistently observed lineage diversification within N. subflava populations.
This phenomenon most likely results from the interplay of subtle spatial microgradients (in
nutrients, oxygen, or antibiotic exposure) and intrinsic regulatory processes, such as stochastic
gene expression, phase variation, and the action of small RNAs and transcription factors.
Despite planktonic processing, transient micro-aggregates and surface-adherent
subpopulations likely create local biofilm-like niches. Enrichment of comP (competence/pilus
assembly) and bamE (BAM-complex assembly) in resistant clusters points to micro-niche
formation and outer-membrane fortification under β-lactam pressure, consistent with β-lactam–
primed biofilm programs rather than reliance on pre-formed biofilms. Adaptive differentiation
may arise even in macroscopically homogeneous cultures due to localized fluctuations in
environmental conditions, most notably within micro-niches that resemble biofilm-like
environments. While antigenic (pilin) variation is a well-documented source of phenotypic
diversity in Neisseria10, our results suggest that the observed transcriptional heterogeneity and
lineage bifurcation primarily stem from adaptive regulatory mechanisms rather than large-scale
antigenic switching (Discussion, lines 423-446).

convergent evolution under ceftriaxone pressure. In contrast, the three C9 strains displayed

subflava. The striking convergence of laboratory and clinical evolutionary trajectories
reinforces the ecological and clinical validity of the adaptive strategies identified here, while
also underscoring the importance of expanded environmental sampling to fully define the
distribution and impact of these resistance mechanisms.
